before.text: When you scrape your knee, the skin cells around the scrape make new cells to fill the gap.
Each new skin cell carries the same 46 chromosomes as the cell it came from.
So how does one cell split into two, without losing a single chromosome?
Mitosis works like sharing a recipe book between two kitchens.
Every page, a chromosome, is photocopied, and each page stays clipped to its copy, like two sister chromatids.
Then the clips come undone, and each kitchen, a new daughter cell, gets one complete, identical book.
Here is the whole path, from one cell on the left to two on the right.
The copying comes first, during interphase, before mitosis even begins.
A common mistake is to think mitosis copies the chromosomes.
In fact the DNA is already copied, so mitosis only separates the copies.
Next comes prophase, the first stage of mitosis.
The chromosomes coil up tight into visible X shapes, and the nuclear envelope breaks down.
That lets spindle fibers, growing from the two poles of the cell, reach the chromosomes.
Now zoom in on metaphase.
Spindle fibers from both poles attach to each chromosome at its centromere, where the sister chromatids join.
Then the chromosomes line up single file across the middle of the cell.
That lineup matters, because it puts one sister chromatid of every chromosome facing each pole.
So what do you think happens when the spindle fibers shorten?
In anaphase, they pull the sister chromatids apart, toward opposite poles.
Once separated, each chromatid counts as its own chromosome.
So each pole ends up with one full set.
Back on the path, telophase follows.
A nuclear envelope forms around each set, and the chromosomes loosen up again.
Last comes cytokinesis, when the cytoplasm divides.
In an animal cell, a cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two, leaving two identical daughter cells.
Now, what happens if one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate in anaphase?
Both chromatids get pulled to the same pole.
So in a human body cell, one daughter cell gets 47 chromosomes, and the other gets 45.
Cells with the wrong number of chromosomes often fail to work properly, or die.
So the cell copies every chromosome first, then mitosis pulls the copies apart evenly, so both new cells match.
One human body cell with 46 copied chromosomes goes in, and two identical cells with 46 each come out.
